analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose to health plans what they charge, what they keep in rebates, and how they steer prescriptions to affiliated pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill has sat in three House committees since its March 2025 introduction with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that employers and insurers hire to run prescription drug benefits. This bill would require PBMs to report to health plans, at least every six months, detailed data on drug claims: what the plan pays the PBM versus what the PBM pays the pharmacy, how much the PBM receives in rebates and fees, how much it keeps, and how much of the business it routes to pharmacies it owns. Plans would have to share summary information with workers on request, and PBMs or plans that fail to report face civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day. The bill is disclosure-only: it does not cap drug prices or ban any pricing practice directly.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees with job-based health coverage, and the employers and unions that sponsor their plans, especially at organizations with 100 or more employees. They gain a clear picture of where their drug dollars go, which gives them leverage to renegotiate PBM contracts, spot hidden markups, and demand cheaper dispensing channels. Independent pharmacies gain indirectly, since the reports would expose how much less PBMs pay them than they charge plans.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must report the gap between what the plan pays them for each drug and what they pay the pharmacy — the 'spread' — plus the rebates and fees they receive from drug makers and how much net spending remains after those concessions.

PBMs must disclose how they steer patients to pharmacies they own or control, including mandatory mail-order and specialty programs, and compare their prices to those of independent pharmacies in the same network.
Plans must provide a summary document to participants on request, and individuals may ask their plan for the claims-level data on their own prescriptions.
Plans, insurers, and PBMs that violate the reporting rules face civil penalties of $10,000 per day of violation, and up to $100,000 per item of knowingly false information.
The bill also requires disclosure of payments to brokers and consultants for steering an employer's pharmacy business to a particular PBM, closing one of the hidden-fee channels in the system.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their corporate parents — the three dominant firms are owned by the insurers CVS/Aetna, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — which would have to open their books on spread pricing, rebate retention, and affiliated-pharmacy steering, and bear the cost of building the reporting systems. Plans and insurers also bear some compliance cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill is transparency-only. It does not cap prices, ban spread pricing, or stop PBMs from keeping a share of manufacturer rebates; relief for consumers depends entirely on employers and plans using the new data to renegotiate.

The most detailed, claims-level reporting applies only to plans covering employers or sponsors with at least 100 employees or participants, and employer-sponsored insurance coverage gets the full detail only if the employer affirmatively elects it each year. Workers at smaller employers receive only aggregate summary documents.

The requirements do not begin until 30 months after enactment, and the standard reporting format itself would not be finalized until 18 months after enactment, so benefits would arrive years after any signing.
The reporting burden is substantial and compliance costs for PBMs, insurers, and plans could be passed back into premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone covered by an employer or union health plan, the potential upside is real: the data would show, drug by drug, where money leaks out of the system, and employers who negotiate with PBMs have repeatedly used exactly this kind of disclosure to win concessions. The honest limitation is that disclosure does not lower anyone's copay by itself — the bill relies on employers and regulators acting on the information, covers smaller employers only weakly, and starts years after enactment. Compared with legislation that caps out-of-pocket drug costs directly, this is a modest but genuinely useful step.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 27, 2025 and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce (the lead), Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means — and no committee has taken it up since, so it is waiting with no scheduled vote while the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI) introduced the Prescription Drug Transparency and Affordability Act on March 27, 2025.
It drew three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat — making sponsorship bipartisan from the start.

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means Committees; referral to multiple committees splits jurisdiction and typically slows a bill.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded in the action history.
The bill would amend three separate laws governing health plans — the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code — which is why it was sent to three committees.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent insurers are better off so far, because none of the reporting requirements exist in law and their current pricing arrangements continue unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 27, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 27, 2025; no action recorded since.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Democrat joined by two Republicans and one more Democrat; no votes have occurred and no member has publicly opposed the bill, so its fate so far reflects committee inaction rather than partisan division.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (the three dominant firms are owned by CVS/Aetna, Cigna, and UnitedHealth)
industries.note: The bill forces PBM disclosure of spread pricing, rebate and fee retention, payments to referring brokers, and steering to affiliated pharmacies, with penalties up to $10,000 per day. PBMs profit from exactly these opaque channels, and public exposure gives employers and regulators the evidence to squeeze them.

industries.industry: Health insurers with vertically integrated PBM businesses
industries.note: The three biggest PBMs sit inside larger insurance companies, so transparency into the PBM segment threatens profits those companies earn from their own pharmacy operations. Insurers and plans also bear compliance costs that may be passed into premiums.

The bill requires side-by-side comparison of what PBM-affiliated pharmacies charge plans versus what independent pharmacies in the same network are paid, exposing underpayment of community pharmacies. Independent pharmacists have been the most vocal backers of PBM transparency.
Firms must disclose payments received for steering an employer's pharmacy business to a PBM, including the identity of recipients, bringing an undisclosed fee channel into the open.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term sponsor's bill sitting with three committees and only three cosponsors faces long odds of a standalone floor vote. Its realistic path is being folded into a larger health or PBM package if congressional interest in PBM regulation grows; otherwise it will sit until the Congress ends.
